claims.text: Premelting and melting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are governed primarily by surface-energy-driven segregation.
Au and Cu segregate to the exterior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles as temperature increases.
Au and Cu segregate because they have lower surface energies and thereby minimize total nanoparticle surface energy.
Surface segregation produces a distinct thin shell enriched in Au and Cu.
The segregated surface shell is less strongly bonded than the nanoparticle core.
The segregated shell has a lower melting point than the core.
Premelting therefore initiates as a liquid-like layer at the nanoparticle surface.
Greater surface segregation can cause full melting to begin at a lower temperature.
Segregation-induced surface premelting accelerates as nanoparticle size decreases.
The relevant initial material includes near-equimolar AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles with diameters of 3–6.5 nm.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are homogeneous solid solutions.
Nanoparticles enriched in low-surface-energy elements should develop more surface segregation than compositionally adjusted controls with smaller surface-energy differences.
Nanoparticles with greater low-surface-energy-element segregation will premelt at significantly lower temperatures than compositionally homogeneous baseline nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with higher surface-to-volume ratios will premelt at lower temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with minimal surface segregation should exhibit delayed surface-premelting onset.
The proposed behavior should hold primarily below approximately 10 nm.
The proposed behavior requires constituent elements with substantially different individual surface energies.
Coalescence can complicate measurement of the premelting-temperature depression.
Statistically equivalent segregation and premelting onset in promoted-segregation and control particles would falsify the hypothesis.
